title: Separating quantum circuits from classical LLMs
authors: Srinivasan Arunachalam, Arkopal Dutt, Hari Krovi, Rik Sengupta
abstract: Modern large language models - transformers and diffusion language models - are built around two canonical algorithmic tasks: prediction and generation. We prove unconditional separations between low-depth quantum computation and the corresponding bounded-resource classical language-model architectures in both regimes. Concretely, we exhibit the following:   1. Distributional separation. We give a distribution that is sampleable by $\textsf{QNC}^0$ circuits (i.e., a family of constant-depth quantum circuits consisting of bounded fan-in gates) that no constant-round diffusion language model ($\textsf{DLM}$) with shallow scheduling and denoising can sample within constant distance, even when allowed sublinear chain-of-thought and output-token revision/remasking events, the very features modern $\textsf{DLM}$s rely on.   2. Functional separation. We exhibit a function computable in $\land \circ \textsf{QNC}^0[\log\log n]$ (i.e., a family of O$(\log\log n)$-depth $\textsf{QNC}^0$ circuits, where $n$ is the input length, followed by a single classical $\mathsf{AND}$ gate) such that any constant-depth decoder-only transformer computing the function must be large: it would have to have width $n^{Ω(1)}$.   Together, our work initiates the study of quantum advantage in the era of large language models.
summary: This paper rigorously proves that low-depth quantum circuits possess computational capabilities fundamentally beyond those achievable by modern large language models (Transformers and DLMs). By showing separations in both the ability to sample certain distributions and the complexity of computing specific functions, it initiates a formal study of quantum advantage within the AI domain.
main_problem: To establish unconditional separations between low-depth quantum computation ($	ext{QNC}_0$) and classical Large Language Model (LLM) architectures like Transformers and Diffusion Language Models (DLMs).
main_result: The authors prove both distributional separation (a specific distribution sampleable by $	ext{QNC}_0$ but not by constant-round DLMs) and functional separation (a function computable by shallow quantum circuits requiring a prohibitively large width in any constant-depth transformer).
method: The work employs complexity theory, constructing specific computational tasks (distribution sampling and function computation) to compare the inherent power of bounded-depth quantum gates versus the resource scaling (width $H_{dp}$) of modern LLMs.
model_or_system: The models compared are low-depth quantum circuits ($	ext{QNC}_0$) and classical neural network architectures, specifically decoder-only Transformers and Diffusion Language Models. The analysis focuses on their computational capacity under shallow depth constraints.
key_observables: Distributional distance (for sampling), required width ($H_{dp}$) for functional computation, and circuit depth ($	ext{QNC}_0$ depth).
important_parameters: Constant depth, $\mathcal{O}(\log \log n)$ depth, input length $n$, and the resource metric $H_{dp}$.
main_assumptions: The separations are based on specific complexity-theoretic tasks designed to highlight structural differences between quantum computation and LLM mechanisms.
paper_structure: The paper develops arguments by first establishing foundational separations between $	ext{QNC}_0$ and classical circuits, then extending this comparison specifically to the operational constraints of modern DLMs (including revision/remasking steps) for both distributional and functional tasks.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses quantum advantage in the context of state-of-the-art AI models, providing theoretical benchmarks for when quantum computation might outperform classical deep learning methods.
